items.title: [Feature]: visualize dependencies
items.body:
## What would you like HADocs to do?
Show relations between entities (including helpers and automations) in a visual dependency map

## Why would this be useful?
Easily identify orphaned helpers, impact of changes, unexpected relations and much more.

## Example
https://github.com/polprog-tech/EntityMap

Use case 1:
I have two sets of solar panels and a few helper groups to combine the two sets. Some  automations and helpers still refer to each set individually instead of the groups. Automations are relatively easy to find. Template helpers are near impossible to find. 

Use case 2:
I want to replace my weather integration, it would take a lot of time to record each entity currently in use and migrate everything over. A visual aid would help a lot. 

Use case 3:
Spot circulair dependencies. 

Use case 4:
Notice unexpected things which are hard to spot in code or tables.

items.title: Make visualization dependencies optional to avoid constraining core users to NumPy 1.x
items.body:
Hi! 

My team makes extensive use of your package, neo4j-parallel-spark-loader. 
We’re trying to upgrade to PyArrow 26.0.0 to address CVE-2026-92287, but the loader’s numpy<2 requirement blocks the NumPy 2 version that PyArrow 26 needs in our environment.

In the installed version, I only found a NumPy import in visualize/heatmap.py, alongside Matplotlib and Seaborn. **Would you consider making the heatmap dependencies an optional [visualization] extra**, so installations that don’t use visualization aren’t constrained to NumPy 1.x?

That would remove an important blocker for us.

items.title: Extract and visualize dependencies
items.body:
### Please describe your feature request

Great package Konrad! I love it and find it very useful for complicated projects.

One thing that I was missing every now and then was a way to extract and maybe visualize dependencies of a file/function.

Do you think something like this is worth adding to `box`?
I'd be happy to create a proper draft PR (with less dependencies, cleaner code, tests, etc).

# Quick Example

A quick-and-dirty function I threw together looks like this: `get_box_dependencies ` which either takes a file or a text and reports its dependencies:

```R
library(stringr)

# extracts the box dependencies from a file or a text string
get_box_dependencies <- function(file = NULL, text = NULL) {
  stopifnot(
    "Either file or text must be provided but not both" = xor(is.null(file),
                                                              is.null(text)))
  if (!is.null(file)) text <- paste(readLines(file), collapse = "\n")
    
  # remove commented code
  x <- text |> str_replace_all("#[^\\n]+", "")
  
  # extract box dependencies
  box_txt <- str_extract_all(x, "(?<=box::use\\()[^\\)]*") |> 
    unlist() |> 
    paste(collapse = "\n") |> 
    str_replace_all("\\n", " ")
  
  if (nchar(box_txt) == 0) {
    return(tibble::tibble(
      type = character(0),
      dependency = character(0),
      exports = list(),
      exports_agg = character(0)
    ))
  }
  # [a-zA-Z0-9\\.\\/]+   Name regex for the packages/files
  # (\\[[^\\]]+\\])?     Maybe followed by text in []
  deps <- str_extract_all(box_txt, "[a-zA-Z0-9_\\.\\/]+(\\[[^\\]]+\\])?")[[1]]
  is_file <- str_detect(deps, "\\/")
  
  reps_res <- deps |> str_replace_all("\\[[^\\]]+\\]", "")
  export_names <- deps |>
    str_extract_all("(?<=\\[)[^\\]]+(?=\\])") |> 
    sapply(str_split, pattern = ", *")
  
  tibble::tibble(
    type = ifelse(is_file, "file", "package"),
    dependency = ifelse(!endsWith(reps_res, ".R") & is_file,
                        paste0(reps_res, ".R"), reps_res),
    exports = export_names,
    exports_agg = sapply(export_names, \(x) paste(unlist(x), collapse = " "))
  )
}
```
An example of this function is this
```R
test_string <- "
box::use(
  pkg1[fun1, fun2,
       fun3, fun4],
pkg2[...],
  pkg3
# pkg4[fun5] not used
)

box::use(
  ./file1 ,
  ./file2[ffun1, ffun2,
          ffun3],
  folder/file3[...]
)
"
get_box_dependencies(text = test_string)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   type    dependency     exports    exports_agg          
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <list>     <chr>                
#> 1 package pkg1           <list [1]> "fun1 fun2 fun3 fun4"
#> 2 package pkg2           <list [1]> "..."                
#> 3 package pkg3           <list [0]> ""                   
#> 4 file    ./file1.R      <list [0]> ""                   
#> 5 file    ./file2.R      <list [1]> "ffun1 ffun2 ffun3"  
#> 6 file    folder/file3.R <list [1]> "..."   
```

A larger (but non-reproducible) example output is this code which lists all dependencies and its connections in a directory `app/`

```R
 files <- list.files("app", pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE, recursive = TRUE)
> res <- purrr::map_dfr(files, get_box_dependencies, .id = "file") |> 
+   dplyr::mutate(file = files[as.numeric(file)])
> res
# A tibble: 116 × 5
   file             type    dependency   exports    exports_agg                                  
   <chr>            <chr>   <chr>        <list>     <chr>                                        
 1 app/logic/misc.R package shiny        <chr [1]>  div                                          
 2 app/logic/misc.R package shinyWidgets <chr [1]>  downloadBttn                                 
 3 app/logic/misc.R package data.table   <chr [1]>  ...                                          
 4 app/logic/misc.R package dplyr        <chr [1]>  group_by                                     
 5 app/main.R       package shiny        <list [1]> div h1 NS tagList moduleServer sliderInput i…
 ```

**Caveats** to the solution above:

- this does not work when `box` is used within a function. Eg the following `bar` dependency is picked up but is not reported to belong to `foo`

```r
#' @export
foo <- function(...) {
  box::use(bar[baz])
}
```

- At the moment the function depends on `stringr` and `tibble` (to a lesser degree) and lots of regex. This can be brought down if needed.

items.title: Visualize dependencies in development pod
items.body:
Hi, I would like to visualize dependencies in a swift pod. Is there a way?

I tried:
1. `pod lib create HelloLib`, choose Swift
2. `cd HelloLib`
3. `open Example/HelloLib.xcworkspace`
4. Add logic in Development Pod and use the lib in the demo app. For example, in Development Pod add:
* `public class HelloLib { let dummy = Dummy(); public func doNothing() { dummy.doNothing() }}` 
* `class Dummy { func doNothing() {}}`  
* then, in AppDelegate, import HelloLib and call `HelloLib().doNothing()`
* build the example app
5. `git clone https://github.com/PaulTaykalo/objc-dependency-visualizer.git`
6. `cd objc-dependency-visualizer`
7. `./generate-objc-dependencies-to-json.rb -w -s "" > origin.js`

`Index.html` shows (as expected) AppDelegate, ViewController and HelloLib but no sign of Dummy.

Regards

items.title: Visualize requirement dependencies â€” US-004-02-02
items.body:
# Visualize requirement dependencies â€” US-004-02-02

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Issue ID** | FE-ISSUE-US-004-02-02 |
| **Parent Epic** | EPIC-004 â€” Requirement Analysis & Management |
| **Parent Feature** | FEAT-004-02 Requirement Organization |
| **Parent Story** | US-004-02-02 â€” As a **Bid Manager**, I want requirement dependencies detected and visualized, so that I understand the impact of related requirements. |
| **Class** | F |
| **Priority** | P2 (5 pts) |
| **Labels** | `FE`, `epic/EPIC-004`, `story`, `priority-p2`, `class-f`, `bd-10` |
| **Milestone** | M3 Requirements |

## Business Context

Requirements are rarely independent â€” a mandatory block A gates block B. Visualizing dependencies lets bid managers reason about change impact before committing to a proposal strategy. This issue surfaces detected dependencies; the *write/commit* of analytic dependencies is a backend work item (`BD-10`) and is explicitly out of scope.

## Problem Statement

Even with detection endpoints present, dependency data is invisible without a graph + impact view, and the read surface must not imply writable edges the backend does not implement.

## Current State

Greenfield frontend (`rfp-response-platform-frontend`). Platform shell and shared primitives are delivered by the foundation issues (FE-FOUND-01â€¦08) and must exist first. Dependency endpoints exist on contract Â§7.5 (read-side); the write/commit path is backend-blocked (`BD-10`).

## Target State

`/requirements/{requirementId}/dependencies`: interactive `DependencyGraph` (lazy-loaded, heavy rendering), an `ImpactPanel` listing affected requirements, and a cycle alert. Read-only by design â€” no edge-writing UI ships until `BD-10` resolves.

## Frontend Design References

| Doc | Location |
|---|---|
| Feature design | `engineering/frontend/frontend-implementation-map.md` â€” FE-RE-05 `requirements.py` |
| Component design | `frontend/technical/components/component-implementation-design.md` |
| API contract | `frontend/technical/api/frontend-api-contract.md` Â§7.5 (Requirements BC4) |
| Routing design | `frontend/technical/routing/routing-design.md` `/requirements/{requirementId}/dependencies` |
| State design | `frontend/technical/state/state-management-design.md` |
| Auth design | `frontend/technical/authentication/authentication-design.md` |
| Authorization design | `frontend/technical/authorization/authorization-design.md` (guard: `requirement_read`) |
| Engineering story | `autorfp-engineering/03-user-stories/USER_STORIES_INDEX.md` â€” US-004-02-02 |

## Backend API References

| Method | Path | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/v1/requirements/{id}/dependencies/...` | per-requirement dependency edges â€” verified Â§7.5 |
| POST | `/api/v1/requirements/auto-detect` | run background dependency scan â€” verified Â§7.5 |
| GET | `/api/v1/requirements/dependencies/cycles` | cycle list â€” verified Â§7.5 |
| GET | `/api/v1/requirements/dependencies/impact` | impact surface â€” verified Â§7.5 |

Write/commit of dependencies (`POST /api/v1/requirements/dependencies` create) is **backend-blocked (`BD-10`)** â†’ no write UI in this issue.

## Implementation Tasks

- [ ] `DependencyGraph` (heavy, lazy-loading at route level) rendering outgoing/incoming edges
- [ ] `ImpactPanel` for affected requirements w/ severity ordering + count
- [ ] Dependency scan trigger (`POST /requirements/auto-detect`) via `useRunDependencyScan` + progress card
- [ ] Cycle alert pill from `/requirements/dependencies/cycles`
- [ ] Read/gated page with explanatory "read-only pending backend" touch: no edge controls
- [ ] MSW tests + Storybook (empty graph, dense graph, cycle alert, error)

## Pages & Routes

- Primary: `/requirements/{requirementId}/dependencies` (FE-RE-05).
- Accessible from the requirement detail page (`/requirements/{id}`, US-004-01-03) via action.

## Components

`DependencyGraph` (lazy import via `next/dynamic`), `ImpactPanel`, `DepScannerCard`, `CycleAlert`, `StatusChip`.

## Hooks & State

`useRequirementDependencies`, `useDependencyImpact`, `useDependencyCycles`, `useDependencyScan` (job submit), `useJobStatus` reuse from FE-FOUND.

## API Integration

- `GET /api/v1/requirements/{id}/dependencies/*` â€” edges feed the graph.
- `POST /api/v1/requirements/auto-detect` â€” trigger scan; poll status; or simply refresh GET results.
- `GET /api/v1/requirements/dependencies/cycles` + `impact`.
- No write endpoints (BD-10). Contract Â§7.5 reference only; no invented paths.

## Files Expected to Create

```
src/app/requirements/[requirementId]/dependencies/page.tsx
src/components/requirements/DependencyGraph.tsx
src/components/requirements/ImpactPanel.tsx
src/components/requirements/CycleAlert.tsx
src/lib/queries/requirementDependencies.ts
```

## Files Expected to Change

`src/components/requirements/RequirementDetailPage.tsx` (add "Dependencies" action) â€” see list from US-004-01-03.

## Testing Requirements

- Unit: impact ordering; cycle detection display.
- Storybook: graph states (empty, loaded, error, with edges).
- MSW: graph fetch, auto-detect job flow, cycle payloads.
- E2E (subset): open a graph from a detail page, verify no write controls anywhere.

## Acceptance Criteria

(from engineering story intent â€” must be demonstrably met in UI)

- [ ] Detect + visualize requirement dependencies (edges + direction)
- [ ] Impact panel lists affected requirements with severity
- [ ] Cycles surfaced so users see blocking rings
- [ ] Page is read-only (BD-10 write/commit path is backend-block from this issue)

## Definition of Done

- Chrome, Firefox, Safari (latest stable) render correctly; no regression.
- LEES (loading, empty, error, success) for every async surface.
- Responsive at 1440px and 768px; no horizontal overflow.
- WCAG 2.1 AA (contrast, keyboard, focus visible, labels, landmarks).
- `eslint` zero errors; `tsc` strict zero errors; production build passes.
- Consumes only verified endpoints (contract Â§7.5); no invented endpoints; `BD-*` documented.
- i18n strings externalized; axe-core scan 0 critical/serious.
- Reviewer (not implementer) verifies story AC; UI gap log updated.

## Dependencies

- FE-FOUND-01â€¦08 (Phase 0 â€” DataTable, LEES, lazy-load primitives).
- Backlog: US-004-01-01/03 (requirement set via detail).

## Backend Dependencies

BD-10 â€” write/commit of dependency edges is blocked (contract Â§7.5 lists candidates/read-only; "merge apply" still referred). The issue ships read-only; issue marked `bd-10` so the blocker is visible on the story board.

items.title: [FEAT] Timeline: vertical row reordering for projects and tasks

labels.name: status:needs-confirmation
labels.description: Fix landed; awaiting reporter or release confirmation

items.body:
### Target platform
Desktop

### Area
UI / accessibility / i18n; Planner / Timeline

### What problem are you trying to solve?
In the Timeline view, projects and tasks are displayed according to default or date ordering. Users cannot manually reorder or prioritize the vertical cascade of projects or child tasks on the Timeline to visualize dependencies or custom workflow sequences.

### Proposed solution
- Support dragging project and task rows vertically within the Timeline view.
- Persist the chosen order (e.g. updating the project or task orderNum / display order).
- Maintain visual hierarchy (e.g. keeping child tasks grouped under their parent projects if applicable).

### Additional context
Being able to reorder Timeline rows allows users to arrange dependent roadmap projects in chronological cascade sequence without having to artificially adjust dates.

items.title: Add deterministic crowd-instance SVG proof and manifest
items.body:
## Goal
Create a small Visualize-owned integration fixture for the current Extremus crowd-layout output shape. Prove resource resolution and repeatable CPU/SVG manifestation before integrating a pinned bake from the Gestures owner.

## Scope
- Use a deterministic, hand-authored set of instance records matching the currently documented bake shape; do not claim this consumes Gestures' actual bake until a pinned cross-repository fixture is available.
- Reuse the existing public Visualize geometry/material/instance-buffer/frame/resource-provider contracts and GUI.SVG backend.
- Emit an SVG capture and machine-readable manifest that separates represented population, instances iterated, draw commands, resource revisions, and output bytes.
- Add repeatability and resource-resolution assertions and run them in CI.
- Document clearly that this is a CPU/SVG contract proof, not GPU instancing, pose animation, or a population-scale benchmark.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Fixture builds against existing development contracts without adding Visualize dependencies to Gestures.
- [ ] Same input produces deterministic manifest and stable SVG output (excluding any explicitly documented nondeterministic metadata).
- [ ] Missing/invalid resources fail visibly and are covered by tests.
- [ ] CI validates the manifest and publishes the SVG/manifest artifacts.
- [ ] Handoff requests a pinned golden bake from the Gestures owner after this consumer-side fixture is green.

## Boundaries
Visualize owner only. Do not edit Gestures, Physics, WebPage-owned code, or master. Work on development; no package publication.

items.title: [Phase 0] Decide broker protocol and read-only visualizer feed (ADR-0003)
items.body:
## Goal
Choose the integration transport and a safe, narrow feed from backend state/events to the browser visualizer.

## Dependencies
- #2 — Selected local stack.
- #3 — Domain boundaries and state ownership.

## Scope
- Compare a small number of suitable broker/transport options for a local demo.
- Decide how commands flow to the machine simulator and how normalized state/events reach the visualizer.
- Define a read-only feed approach (for example SSE/WebSocket/polling, selected only with evidence).
- Ensure the browser never receives privileged broker credentials or direct database access.
- Record message delivery assumptions, reconnection/stale-data behavior, and local test strategy.

items.title: Visualize status dependencies as a graph
Validate Custom Visualizations Between Stage and Production (with LookML Manifest Fallback)
items.body:
### Summary
Add validation for custom visualizations between **Stage** and **Production** to ensure dashboards, Looks, and LookML content promoted to Production do not break due to missing visualization dependencies.

Because custom visualizations can be provisioned at the instance level (via Admin/Marketplace) or declared directly in LookML (`manifest.lkml`), a new visualization declared in `manifest.lkml` will not appear in Production's API until **after** the release is deployed to Production. The validation must account for this by checking `manifest.lkml` before flagging any visualization missing in Production as an error.

### Background & Context
When promoting user-defined dashboards (UDDs), Looks, or releasing LookML models from Stage to Production:
- If a custom visualization is configured on Stage but missing from Production, tiles using that visualization fail to render.
- However, comparing Stage and Production visualizations purely via the Looker API prior to deployment introduces false positives: when an engineer adds a new custom visualization in `manifest.lkml` as part of the release, that visualization is not registered on the Production instance until `deploy_ref_to_production` executes.
- The validation check must distinguish between genuine instance drift (missing from Prod API and not in the deployment manifest) versus planned LookML additions (missing from Prod API but declared in `manifest.lkml`).

### Requirements
- **Scope**: Validate custom visualizations strictly between **Stage** and **Production** (during release pre-flight checks and/or parity workflows).
- **API Inspection**: Fetch active custom visualizations from Stage and Production instances (via Looker API / `looker-cli`).
- **Manifest Fallback Parsing**:
  - Parse `manifest.lkml` in the repository for `visualization: { id: ... }` blocks.
  - If a visualization exists on Stage but is missing from Production via the API, check if it is defined in `manifest.lkml`.
  - If defined in `manifest.lkml`, treat it as pending deployment (valid / non-blocking).
  - If missing from both Production API and `manifest.lkml`, fail the validation and report the missing visualization dependency.
- **Parity & Discrepancy Checks**: Compare configuration attributes (such as `label`, `url`/`file`, dependencies) for visualizations present across environments or in the manifest to flag configuration drift.
- **Reporting & Diagnostics**:
  - Produce a structured diagnostic report (JSON status report and GitHub Actions Step Summary).
  - Clearly categorize visualizations into:
    - In Sync (present on both Stage and Prod)
    - Pending Deploy (declared in `manifest.lkml`, awaiting Prod deployment)
    - Missing in Prod (unresolved drift / missing dependency failure)

items.title: Provide the supported scientific Python interface, matching CLI and reproducible recipes
items.body:
## Context

Darwin is the sole owner of reusable science. Current research/publisher modules are not yet a stable integration contract, and broad dependencies/editable sibling checkouts are unsuitable production prerequisites.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Specify a supported Python interface and matching CLI backed by the same implementation, including documented errors and compatibility policy.
- [ ] Define Darwin-owned versioned recipe/result contracts and fixtures for exact source identities, selections, ordered operations/parameters, software versions and scientific status.
- [ ] Execute and reproduce a recipe without the dashboard, a mandatory Darwin server, CJC or Slurm.
- [ ] Cover cut/crop/select/integrate/assemble and declared transformations through a documented operation inventory; unsupported operations fail explicitly rather than silently approximating.
- [ ] Declare direct runtime dependencies (including publisher YAML support), isolate optional research/native/visualization dependencies, and test an installed release from an empty directory without sibling checkouts.
- [ ] Prove Python/CLI equivalence, recipe roundtrip and actionable structured failures through the supported interface.

## Design authority and scope

Approved four-project agreement revision 1 (2026-10-25); local specification: `docs/integration-spec.md`. The specifications/agent guidance were prepared locally and must be landed/reviewed alongside implementation; this ticket is self-contained and does not assume those files already exist on the default branch. Producer-owned formats/field names are implementation decisions, not already-settled contracts. This ticket requests planned implementation/review, not permission to deploy, submit cluster jobs, change scientific settings, or rewrite immutable evidence.

## Coordination

Tracked by: https://github.com/benatouba/darwin-wrf-setups/issues/37

## Revision-2 audit follow-through (2026-10-29)

Keep independent packaging/compatibility as the owner scope; add consumer CI and unique future candidate identity/runtime restoration evidence through https://github.com/benatouba/darwin/issues/20 and https://github.com/benatouba/darwin/issues/19. Historical candidate artifacts/receipts remain unchanged.

Authority: maintainer-approved revision 2, SSH-only deployment transfer with operator-created keys kept out of every repository; no deployment/scientific changes authorized by this documentation task.

items.title: bug(cli): visualizer queries use LIMIT without ORDER BY — the same graph draws a different subset depending on insertion order (0/80 rows in common)
items.body:
## Problem

The `cgc ... --visual` queries in `src/codegraphcontext/cli/visualizer.py` cut their result with `LIMIT` but have no `ORDER BY`. When more rows match than the limit, the rows you get depend on the storage order, which changes when the graph is built in a different order (re-index, different file discovery order, another backend). The same code and the same graph can draw a different subset each time.

Queries with `LIMIT` and no `ORDER BY` (line numbers on upstream/main `1b595a61`):

| File:line | Function | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| `cli/visualizer.py:80` | `visualize_search_results` (pattern) | 80 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:89` | `visualize_search_results` (type) | 80 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:94` | `visualize_search_results` (name) | 80 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:110` | `visualize_call_graph` (incoming) | 120 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:115` | `visualize_call_graph` (outgoing) | 120 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:138` | `visualize_call_chain` | 200 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:152` | `visualize_dependencies` | 120 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:170` | `visualize_inheritance_tree` (the `LIMIT` binds only to the second `UNION` arm) | 120 |
| `cli/visualizer.py:183` | `visualize_overrides` | 120 |
| `cli/cli_helpers.py:651` | `_OFFLINE_VIZ_DEFAULT_QUERY` | 300 |

Some related spots have an `ORDER BY`, but it leaves ties, so the cut is still arbitrary among the tied rows:

- `cli/main.py:2292` and `:2305` (`cgc find pattern`): `ORDER BY n.is_dependency ASC, n.name LIMIT 50`. Same-named functions/classes in different files tie.
- `tools/code_finder.py:950` (`get_class_hierarchy` methods, which `cgc analyze tree` slices to `[:10]`): `ORDER BY method_is_dependency ASC, method_line_number`.
- `core/simulator.py:547` (hotspots, which callers show the first N of): sorts on `hotspot_score` only.
- `tools/query_tool_languages/java_toolkit.py`:
  - `:81` orders on `http_path, http_method`;
  - `:122` orders on `stereotype, name`;
  - `:155` orders on `injector.name`;
  - `:186` orders on `fn.path, fn.line_number`;
  - `:251` orders on `c.resolution_tier DESC`.

  All of these are followed by `LIMIT`, and none of them identify a row.

### Repro (upstream/main 1b595a61, no code changes)

The script builds the same graph twice, inserting the nodes in ascending order in one database and in reverse order in the other. The graph is 200 files, each with one `handler` Function that CALLS `target`, plus one Class that CONTAINS the `handler`. The script then captures the visualizer's query (`_launch_visualizer` monkeypatched), runs it on both databases, and compares the returned rows.

```python
from codegraphcontext.cli import visualizer as V
sent = []
V._launch_visualizer = lambda q, **_: sent.append(q)
V.visualize_search_results([], "handler", search_type="name")
V.visualize_call_graph([], "target", direction="incoming")
V.visualize_overrides([], "handler")
# for order in (range(200), reversed(range(200))): fresh KuzuDBManager / LadybugDBManager,
#   CREATE (:Function {name:'handler', path:f'/r/f{i:03}.py'}) -[:CALLS]-> target, (:Class)-[:CONTAINS]->(handler)
#   then run each captured query and collect the returned n.path values
```

Results: Kùzu 0.11.3 and LadybugDB 0.19.1, run in separate processes, gave identical results.

| Query | Rows (asc / reversed) | Rows in common |
|---|---|---|
| search by name (`LIMIT 80`) | 80 / 80 | **0** (`f000..f079` vs `f120..f199`) |
| call graph incoming (`LIMIT 120`) | 120 / 120 | **40** |
| overrides (`LIMIT 120`) | 120 / 120 | **40** |

The data is the same and only the insertion order differs, yet the two runs draw entirely different nodes.

## Impact

- Whenever the match count exceeds the limit, the visual output of `cgc find`, `cgc analyze calls/callers/chain/deps/tree/overrides --visual` and the offline viz default is a storage-order-dependent subset. It can change after a re-index or between backends with no change to the code.
- The tied `ORDER BY`s in `cgc find pattern`, `get_class_hierarchy`, hotspots and the Java toolkit have the same problem, limited to the tied rows.
- Any snapshot or parity comparison of these outputs across backends or re-indexes is flaky.

## Proposed fix

- End each limited query with an `ORDER BY` that identifies a row: the node's `path, line_number, name`, plus `rel.line_number` and the other endpoint for edge rows. For example:

  ```cypher
  ... RETURN caller AS n, rel AS rel, target AS m
      ORDER BY n.path, n.line_number, n.name, rel.line_number, m.path, m.line_number, m.name
      LIMIT 120
  ```

  For the `UNION` in `visualize_inheritance_tree`, give each arm its own `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`.
- Extend the tied `ORDER BY`s with the row identity. For example, `cgc find pattern` becomes `ORDER BY is_dependency ASC, name, path, line_number, type`, and the hotspot sort becomes `(-hotspot_score, relative_path)`.
- A cheap guard against regressions is a static test that every Cypher string containing `LIMIT` in `cli/` (and `tools/`) also contains `ORDER BY`, with an explicit allow-list for the cases where order doesn't matter, such as the `clean` delete batches (`WITH n LIMIT $batch_size DETACH DELETE n`).

A downstream fork has fixed this, with such a static test and an embedded-DB test that runs the ordered visualizer queries. That fix sits on fork-specific test infrastructure and a redesigned `visualize_call_chain`/`visualize_dependencies`, so it can't be submitted as-is.

## Related

- #1843: `call_chain` enumerates paths, not edges. That is the same query shape as `visualize_call_chain`'s `MATCH p = (start)-[:CALLS*1..depth]->(end)`.
- #1782 (open) also touches the visualizer, but only `viz/server.py` Windows path handling. It doesn't touch these queries.

items.title: [FEATURE] GPU Utilization Monitoring During Training
items.body:
## GPU Utilization Monitoring During Training

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
We need to measure GPU utilization during training workloads to identify bottlenecks. Current benchmarks measure throughput but don't show if GPUs are being fully utilized or if there are data loading/networking issues causing idle time.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add a new `utilization` benchmark or extend `burn` to measure:
- **Average GPU Utilization**: % of time GPU is active (target: >85%)
- **Memory Utilization**: % of VRAM used during training
- **SM Occupancy**: Streaming multiprocessor occupancy
- **Data Loading Efficiency**: Time spent waiting for data vs computing
- **Gradient Sync Efficiency**: Time spent synchronizing across GPUs

The benchmark should:
- Monitor utilization during realistic training workloads
- Support various batch sizes and data loading configurations
- Report utilization metrics over time (not just averages)
- Identify bottlenecks (data loading, networking, compute)

**Technical implementation:**
- Use nvidia-smi or CuPy for utilization monitoring
- Sample at regular intervals (100ms-1s)
- Support both single-node and multi-node configurations
- Follow existing BaseBenchmark pattern
- Chart in reporter with time series visualization

**Dependencies:**
- nvidia-smi (already used)
- CuPy (already used)
- No external dependencies

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
1. **nvidia-smi monitoring**: Manual, not integrated
3. **Custom profiling scripts**: Not standardized, hard to reproduce
3. **Framework-specific tools**: PyTorch profiler, TensorBoard

**Additional context**
- Low utilization indicates bottlenecks (data loading, networking)
- Important for infrastructure optimization
- Different from throughput: measures efficiency, not speed
- Target >85% utilization for good GPU efficiency
